title: Shock tube, air at rest released across a pressure jump (Sod's problem)

summary.headline: Verification FAILED on one of its own limits. OpenFOAM's shock solver converges to the exact solution of the shock tube: on 12800 cells the mean errors are \(0.0085\,\%\) (density), \(0.012\,\%\) (velocity), \(0.0068\,\%\) (pressure), the states between the waves are within \(0.0022\,\%\) and mass and energy are kept to round-off. But the pressure error falls more slowly than the limit set before the runs assumed (order \(0.78\) against \(0.85\)): \(0.0068\,\%\) against a limit of \(0.0055\,\%\).

findings: Verdict by the rules written before the runs: FAIL. 16 of 18 rules hold. Broken, FAIL: mean pressure error on the finest grid. Broken, WARN: extra up-and-down of density and pressure (wiggles), every grid of the family.

The simulation converges to the exact solution. From 100 to 12800 cells the mean error falls by \(54\times\) (\(\rho\)), \(70\times\) (\(u\)), \(50\times\) (\(p\)). On the finest grid the uniform states are within \(0.0022\,\%\), the shock within \(0.06\) cells and the border of the two gases within \(0.35\) cells of their exact places.

It converges more slowly than the pressure limit assumed. The limit was sized for an order of \(0.85\); the measured order over the eight grids is \(0.78\). The pressure error on the finest grid is \(0.0068\,\%\) of \(p_L\), the limit \(0.0055\,\%\). The error sits in the expansion fan: \(81\,\%\) of the pressure error and \(51\,\%\) of the density error on the finest grid, falling with order \(0.78\) there. A smaller time step does not reduce it (see the time-step study).
Mass, momentum and energy are kept to round-off on every step of every run (largest relative change \(5.3 \times 10^{-14}\)). This is why the shock sits in the right place on every grid.

Sharpness. The shock is \(1.8\) to \(2.2\) cells wide on every grid, so its width in metres halves with the cell size. The border of the two gases is wider, \(4.4\) to \(6.3\) cells: nothing in the flow pushes it back together once it is smeared.

The time step matters more than the tutorial suggests. At the tutorial's limit (twice the step used here) pressure and velocity between the fan and the shock ripple by \(3.1\,\%\) on 400 cells; at the step used here by \(0.6\,\%\). The ripple does not go away with a finer grid: it is \(0.6\,\%\) on 12800 cells.

Choice of limiter (400 cells): the tutorial's van Leer limiter has the lowest density error of the six combinations tried. The first-order scheme smears the border of the two gases over \(21\) cells; SuperBee keeps it to \(2.4\) cells but doubles the error in the fan.
limitations: One of the limits set before the runs is not met (pressure on the finest grid), so the verdict is FAIL. The limit rested on my expectation that pressure would converge with an order of at least \(0.85\). Whether the measured \(0.78\) is a property of this solver's scheme or of any method of this kind was not settled: only one solver was run. A second, independent solver on the same grids would tell.

The time step is not converged. On 400 cells the density profile changes by \(0.061\,\%\) of \(\rho_L\) when the step is cut to a quarter, against a total error of \(0.13\,\%\). The error against the exact solution is lowest at the step used here because the time error and the space error partly cancel, not because the time error is small.

The solver's only time scheme (explicit Euler) leaves a ripple of about \(0.6\,\%\) behind the shock at this time step, and the extra up-and-down of the profiles grows slowly with the number of cells (\(2.8\,\%\) to \(5.5\,\%\)).
The grid study was made at one Courant number. The order of convergence at a smaller time step was not measured.
The problem is one-dimensional, without viscosity, and ends before any wave reaches a wall. Reflections, boundary layers and the bursting of a real diaphragm are outside it.

With an error that falls like the cell size to the power \(0.8\), accuracy is expensive: ten times less error needs about \(17\) times more cells, and in one dimension the time steps grow with the cells, so about \(289\) times more work.

Statements about published methods (the flux scheme, the expected order at a jump) are cited from memory, not from references supplied with the problem: G. A. Sod, J. Comput. Phys. 27 (1978) 1–31; A. Kurganov, S. Noelle and G. Petrova, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 23 (2001) 707–740; C. J. Greenshields, H. G. Weller, L. Gasparini and J. M. Reese, Int. J. Numer. Meth. Fluids 63 (2010) 1–21; J. W. Banks, T. Aslam and W. J. Rider, J. Comput. Phys. 227 (2008) 6985–7002.

problem.description: A closed tube of air is divided by a thin wall. The air on the left is at ten times the pressure and eight times the density of the air on the right, and all of it is at rest. At time zero the wall is removed. Find how the air moves in the first half millisecond, before any wave reaches an end of the tube, and compare the simulation with the exact solution of this problem.
setup: A straight tube of length \(L\) with closed ends, filled with air at rest. Coordinate \(x\) along the tube, from \(0\) to \(L\). The flow depends only on \(x\) and on time \(t\).
A thin wall at \(x = L/2\) separates two uniform states. Left of it: pressure \(p_L\), density \(\rho_L\). Right of it: pressure \(p_R\), density \(\rho_R\).
At \(t = 0\) the wall is removed instantly.
The air is an ideal gas, \(p = \rho R T\), with a constant ratio of specific heats \(\gamma\).
No viscosity and no heat conduction (the Euler equations). The tube wall and the closed ends are frictionless and let no heat through.
This is the test problem of Sod (1978) in SI units: in units of \(\rho_L\), \(p_L\) and \(L\) the two states are \((\rho, u, p) = (1, 0, 1)\) and \((0.125, 0, 0.1)\).
The problem has an exact solution (the Riemann problem of gas dynamics). It holds until the first wave reaches an end of the tube.

problem.reference: The exact solution of this problem (derived and checked in Theory). The problem is the test of G. A. Sod, J. Comput. Phys. 27 (1978) 1–31.

theory.intro: This problem has an exact solution, so the simulation can be checked against it everywhere, not only at a few numbers. The solution is put together from three pieces, each proven by SymPy below, and one equation for the pressure between the waves, solved numerically in two independent ways. The assembled solution is checked once more as a whole: its mass, momentum and energy at the time of interest equal what the tube started with. One thing theory also says about the simulation: a method that captures jumps over a few cells cannot reach the accuracy it has in smooth flow, so the error should fall roughly in proportion to the cell size, not to its square (see Comparison).

steps.label: Governing equations: mass, momentum and energy of a gas without friction or heat conduction, in one dimension
steps.latex: \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\begin{pmatrix}\rho\\ \rho u\\ E\end{pmatrix} + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\begin{pmatrix}\rho u\\ \rho u^2 + p\\ u(E+p)\end{pmatrix} = 0,\qquad E = \frac{p}{\gamma-1} + \frac12\rho u^2
steps.note: These are the Euler equations. \(E\) is the energy per unit volume. Written like this, each line says: what a slice of the tube holds changes only by what flows in and out through its two faces. That stays true across a jump, where derivatives do not exist.

steps.label: No length or time scale: the solution depends on \((x - x_0)/t\) only
steps.note: Two uniform states meeting at a point have no length scale, so the picture at a later time is the earlier one stretched. Every wave leaves the wall position at a constant speed. Three waves form: an expansion fan to the left, a shock to the right and, between them, the border of the two gases.

steps.label: Left: the expansion fan (a smooth drop in pressure and density)
steps.latex: s = \frac{2}{\gamma+1} - \frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}\,\frac{\xi}{c_L},\qquad \rho = \rho_L\,s^{\frac{2}{\gamma-1}},\quad u = \frac{2}{\gamma+1}\,(c_L + \xi),\quad p = p_L\,s^{\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}}\qquad (-c_L \le \xi \le u^* - c^*_L)
steps.note: \(s\) is the local speed of sound divided by \(c_L\). The velocity rises linearly across the fan. SymPy checks below that these three functions satisfy the three equations above.

steps.label: Right: the shock (a jump), from conservation across it
steps.note: These are the Rankine-Hugoniot relations for a shock moving into gas at rest. SymPy checks below that mass, momentum and energy flowing into the jump equal what flows out.

steps.label: Between them: one pressure and one speed; the density jumps at the border of the two gases
steps.latex: p = p^*,\quad u = u^*\quad (x_{\mathrm{tail}} < x < x_{\mathrm{shock}}),\qquad \rho = \rho^*_L\ \ (x < x_{\mathrm{contact}}),\quad \rho = \rho^*_R\ \ (x > x_{\mathrm{contact}})
steps.note: \(p^*\) follows from requiring that the fan and the shock give the same \(u^*\) (first card below).

self_checks.name: fan: momentum equation \(\partial_t(\rho u) + \partial_x(\rho u^2 + p) = 0\)
fan: each ray \(x - x_0 = \xi t\) moves at the speed of a left-running sound wave, \(\xi = u - c\)
fan: no entropy is made, \(p/\rho^\gamma = p_L/\rho_L^\gamma\)
fan: it starts at the undisturbed gas, \(\rho = \rho_L,\ u = 0\) at \(\xi = -c_L\) (\(s = 1\))
fan: written with \(s = c/c_L\), the velocity is \(u = 2c_L(1 - s)/(\gamma - 1)\)
shock: momentum is conserved across the jump, \(p_1 + \rho_1 S^2 = p_2 + \rho_2 (S - u_2)^2\)
shock: energy is conserved across the jump, \(h_1 + \tfrac12 S^2 = h_2 + \tfrac12 (S - u_2)^2\) with \(h = \gamma p/((\gamma-1)\rho)\)
shock: the gas speed behind it is \(u_2 = (p_2 - p_1)\sqrt{A/(p_2 + B)}\), \(A = 2/((\gamma+1)\rho_1)\), \(B = (\gamma-1)p_1/(\gamma+1)\)
pressure between the waves: SymPy (30 digits) and SciPy (bracketing) agree to \(10^{-12}\) of \(p_L\)
wave pattern: \(p_R < p^* < p_L\), so the left wave is an expansion fan and the right wave a shock
the gas speed behind the shock equals the gas speed behind the fan (one \(u^*\)), to \(10^{-12}\)
the fan ends at the left middle state: at its last ray \(\rho = \rho^*_L\), \(u = u^*\), \(p = p^*\)
the shock compresses and heats: entropy rises, \(p^*/\rho_R^{*\gamma} > p_R/\rho_R^\gamma\)
whole solution at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\): total mass equals the starting mass, to \(10^{-12}\)
whole solution at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\): total energy equals the starting energy, to \(10^{-12}\)
whole solution at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\): total momentum equals the push of the end walls, \((p_L - p_R)\,t_{\mathrm{end}}\), to \(10^{-12}\)
no wave has reached an end of the tube at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\): fan head at \(x > 0\), shock at \(x < L\)

decisions.choice: The Euler equations in one dimension: an ideal gas with a constant ratio of specific heats, no viscosity, no heat conduction, no turbulence model
decisions.why: This is the problem as stated, and the exact solution is a solution of these equations. The viscosity is set to zero (mu 0); the solver then skips its viscous and heat-conduction steps. The specific heat is \(c_p = \gamma R/(\gamma - 1)\), so that the gas has exactly the given \(\gamma\). Tref 0 makes the internal energy \(c_v T\) with no offset, so the solver's total energy is the physical one, \(p/(\gamma-1) + \tfrac12\rho u^2\) per unit volume.
decisions.affects: Defines the equations solved. Real air has a small viscosity, which would give the shock a thickness of well under a micrometre here: far below any cell, so it could not be seen.
decisions.alternatives: A viscous gas (the Navier-Stokes equations): not what the exact solution describes.

decisions.choice: The molar mass is set so that OpenFOAM's gas constant is exactly the given \(R\); OpenFOAM's universal gas constant is measured by a one-step run, not typed in
decisions.why: OpenFOAM takes the molar mass and divides its own universal gas constant by it. That constant is built into the program from two rounded numbers, so its digits are not the textbook ones. run.py advances a 10-cell case by one step and reads the constant back from an undisturbed cell (\(p W/(\rho T)\)). The pre-flight then checks that the solver's start densities are the given ones to 12 digits.
decisions.affects: The start densities and \(\gamma\). With the tutorial's rounded molar mass (28.96) the densities would be off by about 0.03 % and every comparison with the exact solution would carry that offset.
decisions.alternatives: The tutorial's rounded value; a textbook value of the universal gas constant.

decisions.choice: rhoCentralFoam, starting from OpenFOAM's own tutorial of this problem (compressible/rhoCentralFoam/shockTube)
decisions.why: A flow with shocks needs a method that keeps mass, momentum and energy exactly (so that a captured shock moves at the right speed) and that does not ring at a jump. rhoCentralFoam is OpenFOAM's solver built for that: it advances density, momentum and energy directly, with fluxes that need no knowledge of the wave pattern. gpucfd does not apply: it solves flows of constant density.
decisions.affects: Which equations are advanced and how; the exact solution it converges to is the same for any conservative method.
decisions.alternatives: rhoPimpleFoam or sonicFoam (pressure-based, implicit: built for lower speeds, and they smear shocks more); a solver that splits each face into its waves (a Riemann solver, not part of standard OpenFOAM).

decisions.choice: The whole tube, \(0 \le x \le L\), one cell across with empty sides (a one-dimensional model); closed ends: no flow through them (slip), zero gradient for pressure and temperature
decisions.why: The flow depends on \(x\) and \(t\) only, and the tube wall is frictionless, so one cell across loses nothing. A frictionless end lets no gas through and no heat: velocity zero normal to it, no gradient of temperature. The cross-section is \(1\,\mathrm{m} \times 1\,\mathrm{m}\), so that a volume integral is the value per unit of cross-section.
decisions.affects: Sets the problem. No wave reaches an end before the time of interest (Theory), so the end conditions are only there to close the tube; the conservation check confirms that nothing leaks through them.
decisions.alternatives: Open ends as in the tutorial (zero gradient for everything): the same answer until a wave arrives, but gas could then leave, and mass would no longer be a check.

decisions.choice: Start state: air at rest, the left state in the left half and the right state in the right half, set cell by cell with setFields; temperatures from \(T = p/(\rho R)\)
decisions.why: Given in the problem. Every grid has an even number of cells, so the wall at \(x = L/2\) lies on a cell face and the start state is exact on the grid: no cell holds a mixture. The solver takes pressure and temperature as inputs, so the given densities enter through the temperatures.
decisions.alternatives: None (it is part of the problem).

decisions.choice: Equal cells along the tube, 100 to 12800 cells (cell size \(10\) to \(0.078\,\mathrm{mm}\)), refinement ratio 2, eight levels
decisions.why: Ratio-2 refinement gives the observed order of accuracy directly. Equal cells keep that test clean, and the waves move, so there is no fixed place to cluster cells. The first plan had six levels, up to 3200 cells. The pre-flight showed that a cell costs about a third of a microsecond per step, so two more levels were added before any production run: the finest was projected at a minute and a half. Eight levels show whether the order has settled.
decisions.affects: The size of the discretisation error: how many cells each jump is smeared over, in metres.
decisions.alternatives: Cells that follow the waves (adaptive refinement): fewer cells for the same sharpness, but a different tool. Fewer levels.

decisions.choice: Central-upwind fluxes of Kurganov, Noelle and Petrova (Kurganov); face values reconstructed with the van Leer limiter for density, velocity and temperature
decisions.why: The tutorial's choice. Each cell value is extended to its faces with a slope (second order where the flow is smooth); the limiter flattens the slope next to a jump so that no new peak appears. The flux then mixes the two face values with the local wave speeds. Five other combinations are run on one grid to show how much this choice matters (Comparison).
decisions.affects: How many cells a jump is smeared over and whether the profile wiggles next to it. It does not change what the method converges to.
decisions.alternatives: Tadmor flux (more smearing); limiters vanAlbada, Minmod (more smearing), SuperBee (sharper, can square off smooth parts); upwind (first order). All five were run.

decisions.choice: Explicit Euler steps of fixed size: the time of interest divided by 1.8 steps per cell (180 steps on 100 cells, 23040 on 12800), a Courant number of 0.19 on every grid, half the tutorial's step
decisions.why: The solver is explicit: a cell is updated from its neighbours' old values, which is only stable if no signal crosses a cell in one step. The fastest signal of the exact solution is \(u^* + c^*_R = 693\,\mathrm{m/s}\) (Theory); with 1.8 steps per cell it crosses 0.19 of a cell per step. This is the usual Courant number, \((|u| + c)\,\Delta t/\Delta x\). The solver prints half of it (0.097), because it counts differently, so the tutorial's limit of 0.2 is a usual Courant number of about 0.4. The time-step study of the pre-flight tested that step and three smaller ones on 400 cells: at the tutorial's step the pressure behind the shock rings by 2 % and its error doubles; at the step chosen here the ringing is 0.3 %. A fixed step (not the tutorial's adjustable one) makes every run end exactly at the time of interest, writes the snapshots at exact times, and keeps the Courant number the same on every grid, so that the grid study changes one thing only.
decisions.affects: The time error, the ringing behind the shock and a part of the smearing. Euler steps are first order in time, the only choice this solver has. The time error is not negligible: see the time-step study in Comparison.
decisions.alternatives: The tutorial's adjustable step with its limit of 0.2 (rings, and the output times are then not exact). A step two or four times smaller (less ringing, 2 to 4 times the cost, no gain in the error against the exact solution; both tested).

decisions.choice: Schemes for gradients, the viscous stress and diffusion: the tutorial's central schemes, kept because the solver reads them
decisions.why: The solver forms the viscous stress on every step even when the viscosity is zero, so it asks for these schemes. Everything they produce is multiplied by zero.

decisions.choice: No iteration: density, momentum and energy are advanced explicitly (diagonal solver)
decisions.why: With explicit steps each cell's new value is a formula of old values. There is no system of equations to solve and so no iteration error; the step-by-step conservation check confirms it.
decisions.alternatives: None for this solver without viscosity.

decisions.choice: Every run ends at the time of interest, \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\); the physical check is made on every step: total mass and total energy must not change, and the total momentum must equal \((p_L - p_R)\,t\)
decisions.why: The problem asks for the state at one time, so there is nothing to wait for and no steady state to judge. What must hold instead is conservation, step by step: the ends are closed, so mass and energy can only change through an error, and the only force on the air is the pressure on the two end walls, which stays \(p_L\) and \(p_R\) until a wave arrives. All three were written down as checks before the first run, with limits sized from the pre-flight's round-off level.
decisions.affects: Whether a run counts as healthy.
decisions.alternatives: Residuals: an explicit solver has none.

decisions.choice: Fields written at 10 equally spaced times with 15 digits; total mass, momentum and energy recorded after every step
decisions.why: The profiles at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\) answer (a), (b), (c) and (e); the earlier snapshots give the wave speeds as slopes of position against time, which does not assume where the waves started. The totals after every step answer (d). 15 digits, because the conservation check looks for changes in the 13th.
decisions.affects: What is measured and how precisely; not the solution.
decisions.alternatives: Wave speeds from the last snapshot alone (position divided by time): also reported.

decisions.choice: The simulation is compared with the exact cell averages, and each output is read from a profile by a fixed rule that is also applied to the exact solution
decisions.why: A finite-volume solver holds the average of density, momentum and energy over each cell, not the value at its centre. In a cell that a jump passes through, the two differ by a large part of the jump. So the exact solution is integrated over each cell (in closed form, Theory), and velocity and pressure are formed from those averages as the solver forms them. The rules for reading states, positions and widths are in numerics.yaml (extraction) and measure.py; reading the exact cell averages with the same rules gives each rule's own bias, reported next to the results.
decisions.affects: The reported errors. With point values instead of cell averages every jump would add an error of up to half a cell that the solver did not make.
decisions.alternatives: Point values of the exact solution at the cell centres (simpler, biased at jumps).

meshes.intro: 16 runs in three studies. Grid: cells doubled seven times, the time step halved with the cell size. Time step: one grid, the step halved three times. Scheme: one grid and step, six ways of building the face values. Every run covers the whole time of interest.

notes: An explicit solver has no residuals to watch. The evidence that each step is right is physical: the total mass and the total energy of the air must not change (closed ends), and the total momentum must equal the push of the two end walls, \((p_L - p_R)\,t\). All three are recorded after every step. Columns: the largest change during the run, relative (Figure 5). Limits: \(1 \times 10^{-11}\).
Ends: the largest relative difference from the start state in the two end cells at the time of interest (limit \(1 \times 10^{-10}\)). It confirms that no wave has reached an end.

Wiggles: the exact density and pressure only fall from left to right. The column is the simulation's total up-and-down above the exact one, so zero means no wiggle at all (limit for the grid study: \(5\,\%\)). It grows slowly with the number of cells, about like the number of cells to the power \(0.18\): the ripple behind the shock keeps its size and covers more cells.
Log checks (cfdlib.monitor): no crash, no NaN, Courant number and its trend. Density and pressure stayed positive in every run.
The grid of every run passed checkMesh.

definitions.name: Mean error (the L1 norm)
definitions.meaning: The mean absolute difference over the cells between the simulation and the exact solution averaged over the same cell. This is the measure to use with jumps: the largest difference never falls, because a cell inside a smeared jump is always wrong by a part of the jump.

definitions.name: Observed order
definitions.meaning: \(p = 1\): halving the cells halves the error. \(p = 2\) would cut it by four.

definitions.name: Width of a jump
definitions.meaning: Distance between the points where the profile has made 10 % and 90 % of the jump, in cells. The same rule applied to the exact cell averages gives \(0.9\) to \(1.6\) cells: that is the rule's own floor.

definitions.name: Wiggles
definitions.meaning: Zero for a profile that only falls from left to right, as the exact density and pressure do.

definitions.latex: \frac{\max q - \min q}{\mathrm{mean}\ q},\qquad q = p,\ u

findings: Order of convergence. Halving the cells cuts the mean error by about \(1.76\times\), not by 2 or 4: orders \(0.81\) (density), \(0.85\) (velocity), \(0.78\) (pressure) over the eight grids (Figure 6). Second order is out of reach with jumps in the solution: a jump spread over a fixed number of cells leaves an error in proportion to the cell size. The surprise is that the order stays below 1.

Where the error is. Not at the shock. On the finest grid the expansion fan holds \(81\,\%\) of the pressure error, \(56\,\%\) of the velocity error and \(51\,\%\) of the density error, and its part falls with order \(0.78\) (pressure), steadily over all grids. The fan is smooth inside, but its two ends are corners, and the scheme rounds them. The limit for the pressure was sized on the assumption that the shock sets the pressure error (order 1 expected, 0.85 allowed); the fan sets it. The shock's own part does fall with order \(0.94\). The slowest part is the stretch around the border of the two gases, where the ripple is: order \(0.54\) for the pressure. It is \(10\,\%\) of the pressure error on the finest grid and would take over on still finer ones.

The time step is not the cause. In the time-step study the fan's part of the pressure error is \(0.12\,\%\), \(0.068\,\%\), \(0.072\,\%\), \(0.08\,\%\) at Courant numbers 0.39, 0.19, 0.10, 0.05: below the step of the grid study it does not fall, it rises a little. I first suspected the ripple behind the shock; the split by wave shows that the ripple is a small part of the error.

The limiter is the cause, in part. With the same grid and time step the density error in the fan is \(0.058\,\%\) (vanLeer), \(0.082\,\%\) (vanLeer, Tadmor flux), \(0.059\,\%\) (vanAlbada), \(0.072\,\%\) (Minmod), \(0.11\,\%\) (SuperBee), \(0.41\,\%\) (upwind). No combination that OpenFOAM offers here does clearly better than the tutorial's.

Time-step error. The error against the exact solution is lowest at the step used for the grid study and rises for smaller steps (Figure 7). So the step is not converged: at a quarter of it the density profile differs by \(0.061\,\%\) of \(\rho_L\), while the total error is \(0.13\,\%\). Time error and space error partly cancel at this step. Because the step is halved with the cell size, both shrink together in the grid study.

Wave positions. On the finest grid the shock is \(0.06\) cells and the border of the two gases \(0.35\) cells from their exact places. The two ends of the fan, read from the straight-line fit, are \(1.4\) and \(1.1\) cells off; the back of the fan is about one cell too far right on every grid (\(0.98\) to \(1.05\) cells), so that error halves with the cell size.

insights.problem: SymPy could not prove that the expansion fan satisfies the Euler equations. Four self-checks came back false although the formulas were right.
insights.diagnosis: The fan's density and pressure are powers of a base with the exponent 2/(gamma-1), kept symbolic. The base was written as an expression in the ray variable, whose sign SymPy does not know, so it refused to combine the powers and the residual did not reduce to zero.
insights.fix: The fan is written with the local speed of sound divided by the left one as the variable, declared positive. The three conservation laws then reduce to zero for any gamma. The entropy check compares logarithms.
insights.lesson: A symbolic proof with non-integer powers needs a base that is a single positive symbol. A check that fails this way says nothing about the physics.
insights.guideline: In the workflow's theory stage, add one line. When a solution has powers with a symbolic exponent (gas dynamics, similarity solutions), write it in a variable that is a positive symbol before asking SymPy to verify it.

insights.problem: OpenFOAM's universal gas constant is not the textbook value, and the tutorial's molar mass of air (28.96) does not give the gas constant of the problem. Typed from memory, the start densities would be wrong by a few hundredths of a per cent.
insights.diagnosis: The solver divides its own universal gas constant by the molar mass. The constant is built into the program as a product of two rounded numbers; a one-step run gave \(8314.47006651\ \mathrm{J/(kmol\,K)}\), where textbooks give 8314.4626. With the tutorial's 28.96 the gas constant is 287.10, not 287.
insights.fix: run.py measures the constant with a 10-cell, one-step run (p W / (rho T) in an undisturbed cell) and sets the molar mass from it. The pre-flight checks that the solver's start densities are the given ones to 12 digits.
insights.lesson: For a compressible case the density is not an input. It follows from pressure, temperature and the solver's own constants, so it has to be checked in the solver's output before anything else.
insights.guideline: Add to the OpenFOAM primer, in a new section on compressible flow, that molWeight must be set from the solver's own universal gas constant, with the measured value for v2606 and the one-step check of the start density. A helper in cfdlib.foam that returns the constant would save every later case of the ladder this step.

insights.problem: The pre-flight copy of a case does not run with the case's time step. monitor.preflight sets the end time with foamDictionary, which rewrites the whole controlDict with 6 digits, so a time step written with 16 digits (the time of interest divided by 180) ran as its 6-digit rounding.
insights.diagnosis: Seen in the total momentum, which is the wall pressure difference times the time. After one step it was 0.2500002 where 0.25 was expected, exactly the rounded time step. The function object also prints its time column with too few digits for a check at round-off level.
insights.fix: The analysis takes the time of each row as step number times the time step read from the case's own controlDict. The momentum check then holds to 15 digits in the pre-flight copy and in production.
insights.lesson: A pre-flight copy edited by foamDictionary is a slightly different case. With a fixed time step chosen to hit an end time exactly, the copy can end one step early or late.
insights.guideline: In cfdlib.monitor.preflight, change the end time without rewriting the file (replace the one entry in the text, or pass writePrecision high enough), and say in the workflow that printed times of function objects carry timePrecision digits only.

insights.problem: The Courant number that rhoCentralFoam prints is half the usual one. The run was planned at 0.19 and the log says 0.097.
insights.diagnosis: The solver forms its Courant number from the face fluxes of its central scheme. In subsonic flow that is (|u| + c) dt / (2 dx), half of the usual (|u| + c) dt / dx (read in its source, centralCourantNo.H, and confirmed by the log). The tutorial's limit maxCo 0.2 is therefore a usual Courant number of about 0.4.
insights.fix: The time step is set from the exact solution's fastest signal with the usual definition, and the report states both numbers.
insights.lesson: A Courant limit copied from a rhoCentralFoam tutorial is twice as large as it looks.
insights.guideline: Add to the primer's compressible section that rhoCentralFoam's printed Courant number is half the usual one in subsonic flow, and that monitor.assess reports the solver's number.

insights.problem: At the tutorial's time-step limit the solution rings behind the shock. On 400 cells, pressure and velocity between the fan and the shock ripple by 3 % (highest minus lowest value), and the pressure error is twice that of half the step.
insights.diagnosis: The solver's only time scheme is the explicit Euler step, which is first order and barely stable with a second-order reconstruction in space. The time-step study on 400 cells shows the ripple falling with the step (3.1 %, 0.6 %, 0.5 % and 0.3 % at usual Courant numbers 0.39, 0.19, 0.10, 0.05). The total variation above the exact one falls from 12 % to 2 %, 1 % and 0.9 %.
insights.fix: The main runs use a usual Courant number of 0.19 (0.097 as the solver prints it), half the tutorial's step, where the ripple is 0.6 %. A limit on the ripple and on the total variation is part of the acceptance rules.
insights.lesson: The time step of rhoCentralFoam is set by the ringing its Euler step makes, not by stability alone. The error against the exact solution is not a good guide here; it was lowest at 0.19 only because the time error and the space error partly cancel.
insights.guideline: Add to the primer that rhoCentralFoam needs a usual Courant number of about 0.2 or less (maxCo 0.1 in its own measure) for a clean shock, with these measured numbers, and that a total-variation check of a profile that should be monotone is a cheap detector. A tool for the ladder would be a solver with a multi-stage time scheme.

insights.problem: The workflow does not say what to compare a finite-volume result with when the solution has jumps. The exact value at a cell centre is the wrong reference in a cell that a jump passes through.
insights.diagnosis: The solver holds cell averages of density, momentum and energy. Next to a jump the exact cell average and the exact centre value differ by up to half the jump, and the error this adds is as large as the error being measured (a few cells times the jump).
insights.fix: The exact solution is integrated over each cell in closed form, and velocity and pressure are formed from the averaged conserved quantities as the solver forms them. Every reading rule (states, positions, widths) is also applied to these exact cell averages, which gives its bias (up to 0.11 cells for a jump's position, 1.3 to 1.6 cells for a jump's width).
insights.lesson: With jumps, compare cell averages with cell averages, and use the mean error (L1), not the largest one.
insights.guideline: Add to the workflow's analysis stage, for flows with shocks. Compare with exact cell averages of the conserved quantities, judge profiles by the L1 error, and measure each extraction rule on the exact solution. cases/shock_tube_sod/theory.py (Exact.cell_averages) and measure.py are the worked example.

insights.problem: The decision check reported blockMeshDict's boundary list as undocumented although a pattern ending in a wildcard after the list's name was given.
insights.diagnosis: cfdlib.foamdict keeps a list (blockMesh boundary, the regions of setFieldsDict) as one setting. Its key is the list's name with nothing after it, so a pattern that expects sub-keys does not match.
insights.fix: The pattern names the list itself.
insights.lesson: A list in an OpenFOAM dictionary is one setting for the checker, whatever it holds.
insights.guideline: One line in report-contract.md under the settings patterns, saying that a list-valued entry is matched by its own name.

insights.problem: The pressure error on the finest grid is above its limit (0.0068 % against 0.0055 % of the left pressure). The limit, written before the runs, assumed that pressure converges with an order of at least 0.85. The measured order is 0.78.
insights.diagnosis: My first explanation was the ripple behind the shock. The data did not support it. Split by wave, 81 % of the pressure error on the finest grid sits in the expansion fan, where it falls steadily with order 0.78. The time-step study shows the fan's part does not fall with a smaller step, and the scheme study shows it depends on the limiter (twice as large with SuperBee). The pre-flight had only two grids (100 and 400 cells), whose single order of 0.94 hid that the order between 200 and 400 cells was already 0.80.
insights.fix: The verdict stays FAIL, as the rule says. The report shows the split by wave, the time-step and scheme studies, and says that the limit rested on a wrong expectation.
insights.lesson: An order measured between two coarse grids is one number and hides its trend. With an exact solution, split the error by region before explaining it; the first explanation here was wrong.
insights.guideline: In the workflow's stage 2, where limits are sized from the coarse pre-flight error and the expected order, ask for three coarse levels when they are cheap, and say that for flows with jumps the L1 error of every quantity can converge with an order below 1 (0.8 here, set by the corners of the expansion fan). A helper in cfdlib.verification that projects the finest error from three coarse levels would make the limit a calculation.

insights.problem: The wiggle measure (total variation above the exact one) grows with refinement, from 1.6 % on 100 cells to 5.5 % on 12800, and crosses its 5 % limit on the finest grid.
insights.diagnosis: The ripple behind the shock keeps its size (0.6 % of the pressure on 400 and on 12800 cells) but covers more cells on a finer grid, and the total variation counts every up and down. So the measure is not independent of the grid; the ripple's size is, and its own limit of 1 % holds.
insights.fix: Reported as a broken WARN rule, with both measures in the health table.
insights.lesson: Total variation is a good detector of wiggles and a poor measure of their size.
insights.guideline: Where the workflow or primer suggests a check for wiggles, recommend the ripple's size on a stretch that should be uniform as the rule, and the total variation only as a detector.

insights.problem: Why the error in the expansion fan falls with order 0.78, not 1, is not established. The back of the fan, read from a straight-line fit of the velocity, is about one cell too far right on every grid and with every second-order limiter.
What the runs cost. The finest grid (12800 cells, 23040 steps) took 84 seconds on one core, and all 16 runs together about two minutes of solver time.
insights.diagnosis: The solver is explicit, so a run costs cells times steps, about 0.3 microseconds per cell and step on the larger grids. Runs below 1000 cells are dominated by start-up (about half a second). The time step is set by the ripple of the Euler step, not by stability. At twice the step the run still holds together but ripples by 3 %.
insights.fix: Nothing to fix in one dimension. Recorded in the performance appendix.
insights.lesson: For this solver the lever on speed is the time scheme, not the work per step. With an error that falls like the cell size to the power 0.8, ten times less error needs about 17 times more cells.
insights.guideline: For the next steps of the ladder (two dimensions, chemistry), carry these two numbers into the cost estimate before choosing grids. A solver with a multi-stage time scheme would be the tool to compare against.

insights.problem: In the summary table, an answer with eight numbers (four waves, each a position and a speed) wrapped in the middle of a number pair and could not be read. One theory card's equation was wider than its card.
insights.diagnosis: The answer columns are narrow and wrap at any space. The equation for the pressure between the waves was written on one line.
insights.fix: Each line of the answer is kept together with a no-wrap span and shorter wave names; the equation is split over two lines.
insights.lesson: An answer with several values per line needs lines that cannot break.
insights.guideline: A helper in cfdlib.report for an answer cell with several lines that do not wrap would save the next case the same trial.

insights.problem: The report server's port 8765 was already taken by another session, and the preview tool started a second server on 8766.
insights.diagnosis: Several sessions share this checkout and one of them already serves the results folder.
insights.fix: Opened the report at port 8765, as the machine file advises. It worked at once.
insights.lesson: This went well only because the machine file says what to do.
insights.guideline: None needed; keep the line in dev-pc.md.

insights.problem: In the theory cards' symbol tables a pressure of 10000 Pa and one of 30313 Pa were printed in computer e-notation (a 1, the letter e and +04), not as numbers.
insights.diagnosis: cfdlib.report.tex_num formats numbers between 0.001 and 100000 with Python's g format and 4 significant digits. A five-digit number then comes out in e-notation, inside math, where the typesetting check does not look. The template applies this to every value of a card's symbol table.
insights.fix: The case passes these values as a float that prints a five-digit number in full (theory.py, class _Shown). A workaround in the case, because the shared tools are not mine to change.

figures.caption: Top: the tube before the wall is removed. Bottom: the tube at the time of interest, with the three waves at their exact positions (to scale along the tube). The arrows show which way each wave moves; the two dotted lines are the front and the back of the expansion fan.

Density, velocity and pressure along the tube at the time of interest. Black: exact solution. Dots: 100 cells (mean density error \(0.45\,\%\)). Blue line: 800 cells (\(0.073\,\%\)). On the finest grid (\(0.0085\,\%\)) the simulation cannot be told from the exact solution at this scale.

Where each wave is at the ten written times. Lines: exact (each wave leaves the wall position at a constant speed). Dots: read from the simulation on 400 cells with the rules of this report. The slope of the dots over the second half of the time gives the wave speeds; on this grid they differ from the exact speeds by at most \(0.19\,\%\) of the shock speed.

The two jumps on 100, 800 and 12800 cells, plotted against the distance from the exact position counted in cells. Left: the shock keeps the same shape in cells on every grid (\(1.8\) to \(2.2\) cells between 10 and 90 % of its height). Right: the border of the two gases is wider and widens a little with refinement (\(4.4\) to \(6.3\) cells). Just right of it the density on the finest grid dips \(2.8\,\%\) below the exact value. The dip is there at every written time, next to the border (\(0.8\,\%\) to \(2.8\,\%\)), so it travels with the gas; its origin was not traced further.

Change of the total mass (solid) and total energy (dashed) since the first step, in parts in \(10^{14}\), on the coarsest and the finest grid. The largest change in any run is \(5.3 \times 10^{-14}\): the last digits a computer carries.

Left: mean error against the number of cells, with lines of order 1 and 2/3 for comparison. Fitted over the eight grids the orders are \(0.81\) (density), \(0.85\) (velocity), \(0.78\) (pressure). The green bar is the limit set for the pressure on the finest grid; the pressure error ends above it. Right: the density error split by wave. On the finest grid the fan holds \(51\,\%\) of it, the border of the two gases \(44\,\%\) and the shock \(5\,\%\); the shock's part jumps up and down because it depends on where the shock sits inside its cell.

Time-step study on 400 cells. Left: pressure between the border of the two gases and the shock for four time steps; the exact value is the black line. The ripple is \(3.1\,\%\), \(0.6\,\%\), \(0.5\,\%\), \(0.3\,\%\) of the pressure at Courant numbers 0.39, 0.19, 0.10, 0.05. Right: mean error against the exact solution. It is lowest at the step used for the grid study (Courant 0.19) and rises again for smaller steps.

Six ways of building the face values, same grid (400 cells) and time step. Left: density across the border of the two gases. Right: pressure behind the shock (the shock is at zero). Widths and errors are in the table below.

performance.intro: One core, one run at a time. The solver is explicit, so the cost of a run is cells times steps, and the steps grow with the cells: each refinement costs four times the one before.
head: Run
Cells
Steps
Solver time (s)
Microseconds per cell and step
CPU busy
notes: On the larger grids a cell costs about \(0.29\) microseconds per step. The small runs are dominated by start-up and by writing the totals after every step (\(22\) microseconds per cell and step on 100 cells).

What limits speed is the time step, not the work per step: the Courant number of \(0.19\) is set by the ripple the Euler step makes: at twice the step the run still holds together but ripples by \(3\,\%\). A time scheme with several stages per step is the usual way to take larger steps without that ripple; OpenFOAM's solver does not offer one, and none was tested here.
All 16 production runs together took \(126\) seconds of solver time; the finest run \(84\) seconds.

In two and three dimensions the same order of convergence makes accuracy much dearer (cells times steps grows like the third and fourth power of the refinement). This is the number to carry to the next steps of the ladder.
